title: EMF & internal resistance
examples: What is the difference between EMF and terminal voltage?
How does the internal resistance affect the current in a battery?
Can you show me a circuit diagram with internal resistance?

explain.say: Today we are learning about electromotive force and internal resistance.
The electromotive force is the maximum voltage supplied by a source.
When current flows, some energy is lost inside the source itself.
The terminal voltage is the actual voltage measured across the external circuit.
So, the relationship connecting these three values is I times the total resistance plus internal resistance equals EMF.
In a real-life example, a car battery supplies power to headlights.

faq.q: What is the difference between EMF and terminal voltage?
faq.a: EMF is the total energy supplied by the source when no current is drawn. The terminal voltage is the voltage actually measured across the external circuit when current is flowing.
asks: What is the source voltage versus terminal voltage?
Does EMF change when I draw current?

faq.q: Why do we have internal resistance in a battery?
faq.a: Internal resistance exists because the chemical reactions inside the battery are not perfectly efficient. This resistance causes some energy to be lost as heat.
asks: What causes energy loss in a power source?

faq.q: How do I calculate the internal resistance from a graph?
faq.a: You can plot terminal voltage against current. The slope of this line will give you the total resistance, R plus r. The y-intercept will give you the EMF.
asks: What does the graph slope represent?

faq.q: Is the internal resistance always the same value?
faq.a: The internal resistance is generally considered a constant value for a specific battery under given temperature conditions. However, it can change with temperature.

faq.q: What is the formula for the terminal voltage?
faq.a: The formula is Vterminal equals EMF minus I times r. This shows the voltage drop due to internal energy loss.
asks: Write the equation for terminal voltage.

facts: EMF is measured in volts, just like potential difference.
Internal resistance causes a voltage drop proportional to the current.
The relationship is EMF equals I times (R plus r).
If the external resistance R is zero, the terminal voltage equals the EMF.

quiz.say: A battery has an EMF of six volts and an internal resistance of one ohm. If it is connected to a circuit with a total external resistance of two ohms, what is the terminal voltage?
quiz.why: First, find the total resistance, which is three ohms. Then, the current is six divided by three, which is two amperes. Finally, the terminal voltage is six minus two times one, which is four volts.

wrong.1: This assumes the terminal voltage equals the current times the internal resistance.
wrong.2: This incorrectly assumes that internal resistance has no effect on the voltage.
wrong.3: This confuses the internal resistance value with the final voltage.

quiz.say: If the current drawn from a source is zero, what is the terminal voltage?
quiz.why: When the current I is zero, the term I times r becomes zero, so the terminal voltage equals the EMF.

wrong.0: This ignores the relationship between the source and the load.
wrong.2: This incorrectly suggests that no voltage is present when no current is flowing.
wrong.3: This confuses the resistance value with the potential difference.

quiz.say: A source provides six volts EMF. When connected to a load, the terminal voltage drops to three volts at a current of two amperes. What is the internal resistance?
quiz.why: The voltage drop is six minus three, which is three volts. This drop is caused by the current times the internal resistance. So, three equals two times r, making r one ohm.

wrong.1: This incorrectly assumes that the voltage drop equals the internal resistance directly.
wrong.2: This mistakes the current value for the internal resistance.
wrong.3: This incorrectly uses the EMF value as the resistance.
